title: Abraham
summary: The patriarch whom God called from Mesopotamia to Canaan with promises of land, offspring and blessing for all the families of the earth; renamed from Abram, father of Ishmael and of Isaac, he is honoured in both Testaments as the model of faith and, for Christians, the father of all who believe.
studyQuestions: What three things does God promise Abram in Genesis 12:1-3, and who, finally, is to be blessed through him?
Genesis 15:6 says Abram believed and it was credited to him as righteousness. What had God just promised him (15:1-5), and what in his circumstances made it hard to believe?
Compare Genesis 12:10-20 and Genesis 16:1-4 with Genesis 22:1-18. What do the earlier stories show about Abraham's fears and shortcuts, and how has his trust grown by chapter 22?
In Genesis 18:22-33 Abraham bargains with God over Sodom. What does he appeal to in verse 25, and what does this teach about bold, honest prayer?
Paul (Romans 4) and James (James 2:21-24) both use Abraham. Which episodes does each one point to, and how can both be true at once?
Hebrews 11:8 says Abraham "went out, not knowing where he went." Where is God asking you to take a next step before you can see the whole road?

title: Abrahamic Covenant
summary: God's covenant with Abraham in Genesis 12-22, promising him descendants, the land of Canaan and blessing for all the families of the earth, sealed by a covenant rite in Genesis 15, given the sign of circumcision in Genesis 17 and confirmed by oath in Genesis 22; the New Testament reads it as fulfilled in Christ, and Christian traditions differ on how its promises to Israel and its sign carry forward.
studyQuestions: What three things does God promise Abram in Genesis 12:1-3 and 12:7, and who, in the end, is meant to be blessed?
In Genesis 15:9-18, who passes between the divided animals, and what does Jeremiah 34:18 suggest that rite meant?
What does God add in Genesis 17 (a new name, an "everlasting covenant", a sign), and why does Paul stress in Romans 4:9-11 that Abraham was counted righteous before he was circumcised?
Galatians 3:17 says the law, coming 430 years later, cannot cancel the promise. What difference does it make that God's promise came first?
Hebrews 6:13-18 says God bound himself with an oath so that his people would have "strong encouragement". Which of God's promises do you find hardest to rest on, and how might Abraham's story help?

title: Acts of the Apostles
summary: The fifth book of the New Testament and the second volume of Luke's two-part work: the story of how the risen Jesus' witnesses, empowered by the Holy Spirit at Pentecost, carried the message about him from Jerusalem through Judea and Samaria to the Gentiles and finally to Rome, centred first on Peter and then on Paul.
studyQuestions: Compare Luke 1:1-4 with Acts 1:1-3. Who is addressed in both, and what does Acts say the "former treatise" was about?
Acts 1:8 names Jerusalem, Judea and Samaria, and "the uttermost part of the earth." Trace where the story is in chapters 2, 8, 10 and 28. How does the book follow that map?
What question brought the apostles and elders together in Acts 15:1-6, and how does the phrase "it seemed good to the Holy Spirit, and to us" (15:28) describe the way they reached a decision?

Acts ends with Paul under guard in Rome yet preaching "with all boldness, none forbidding him" (28:31). Why might Luke end there rather than with Paul's trial, and what does that say about the ongoing story the church still lives in?

title: Babylonian Exile
summary: The deportation of the people of Judah to Babylon by Nebuchadnezzar II in the early sixth century BC — in waves around 597 and 587/586 BC, with the burning of Jerusalem and Solomon's Temple — until Cyrus of Persia allowed exiles to return in 538 BC; the crisis that reshaped Israel's faith and much of the Old Testament.
studyQuestions: According to 2 Kings 24:10-16 and 25:8-12, who was taken to Babylon in each deportation, and who was left behind in the land?
What does Jeremiah tell the exiles to do in Jeremiah 29:4-7, and why might that have surprised people who expected to go home soon?
Psalm 137 asks how anyone can sing the Lord's song in a foreign land. How do Ezekiel 1:1-3 and Isaiah 40:1-2 answer that question in different ways?
Matthew 1:17 divides Jesus's family tree at the exile. What does that tell you about how the first Christians understood where Jesus fits in Israel's story?

1 Peter 1:1 and 1:17 call Christians foreigners and exiles. Where do you feel "away from home" in your own life or church, and what would it look like to seek the peace of the place where God has put you?

title: Barnabas
summary: Joseph, a Levite from Cyprus whom the apostles nicknamed Barnabas, "Son of Encouragement"; a generous early member of the Jerusalem church who vouched for the newly converted Saul, led the young church at Antioch and was sent out with Paul on the first missionary journey.
studyQuestions: According to Acts 4:36-37, what was Barnabas's real name, where was he from, and what did he do with his field?
In Acts 9:26-27, why were the disciples in Jerusalem afraid of Saul, and what did Barnabas tell the apostles about him?
What did Barnabas see when he arrived in Antioch (Acts 11:22-24), and how did he respond?
Compare the order of the names in Acts 13:2 and 13:7 with Acts 13:46. What change in the mission does it hint at?
Barnabas gave Mark a second chance after Mark had left the work (Acts 15:36-39). Who in your church or life might need someone to vouch for them, and what would it cost you to do it?

title: Biblical Canon
summary: The list of books a church receives as Holy Scripture: the "measuring rod" collection that makes up the Old and New Testaments, recognised gradually over centuries and still slightly different in size among Catholic, Orthodox and Protestant Christians.
studyQuestions: In Luke 24:44, which three groups of writings does the risen Jesus say speak about him?
How does 2 Peter 3:15-16 describe Paul's letters, and what does that suggest about how early Christians regarded them?
Why might it matter that the canon was recognised gradually by the whole church, rather than chosen in a single meeting?
If your Bible has fewer or more Old Testament books than a friend's from another tradition, how could you talk about the difference with charity and accuracy?

title: The Binding of Isaac
summary: The account in Genesis 22:1-19 of God testing Abraham by asking him to offer his beloved son Isaac on a mountain in the land of Moriah, of Abraham binding Isaac on the altar, and of the angel who stops him, the ram offered in Isaac's place, and God's renewed oath of blessing; Jews call it the Akedah ("binding"), and Christians have long read it as a foreshadowing of Christ.
studyQuestions: Genesis 22:1 tells the reader something Abraham is not told. What is it, and how does knowing it change the way you read the rest of the chapter?
Isaac asks in Genesis 22:7, "where is the lamb?" Compare Abraham's answer in 22:8 with what happens in 22:13-14. What name does Abraham give the place, and why?
What reasons does the angel give in Genesis 22:12 and 22:16-18 for God's words to Abraham? What does God promise, and for whose sake?
Hebrews 11:17-19 and James 2:21-23 both look back to this chapter. What does each writer draw from it about faith?
Romans 8:32 says God "didn't spare his own Son". Reading Genesis 22 alongside it, what do you learn about the cost of God's love?
Where in your own life is it hardest to trust that "Yahweh will provide", and what helps you keep walking up the mountain?

title: Book of Ezra
summary: The Old Testament book that tells how Jewish exiles returned from Babylon under the Persian king Cyrus, rebuilt the Temple in Jerusalem, and were later led by Ezra, a priest and scribe, to reorder their life around the Law of Moses; in the Hebrew Bible it forms one book with Nehemiah.
studyQuestions: Compare Ezra 1:1-4 with 2 Chronicles 36:22-23. What do the two passages share, and what does that suggest about how the story of Israel continues after the exile?
In Ezra 3:10-13, why do some people shout for joy while older priests and Levites weep at the laying of the Temple's foundation?
What stopped the rebuilding in Ezra 4:24, and according to Ezra 6:14, through whose prophesying did the elders build and prosper?
Ezra 7:10 says Ezra set his heart to seek the law, to do it and to teach it. Why do you think the order of those three verbs matters for anyone who studies Scripture?
Ezra's prayer in chapter 9 confesses the sins of the whole community, not just his own. What might it look like for a church to pray that way today?

title: Book of Jeremiah
summary: The Old Testament prophetic book that gathers the oracles, prayers and life story of Jeremiah, a priest's son from Anathoth who warned Judah from about 627 BC until after Babylon destroyed Jerusalem in 587/586 BC, wrote to the exiles to seek the peace of Babylon, and promised a new covenant written on the heart.
studyQuestions: In Jeremiah 1:4-10, what objection does Jeremiah raise to God's call, and what two kinds of work (tearing down and building up) is he given?
According to Jeremiah 7:1-15, why could the Temple not protect the people of Judah, and what did God want from them instead?
What does Jeremiah 29:4-7 tell the exiles to do in Babylon, and how does verse 11 read differently once you know it was written to people facing seventy years away from home?
Read Jeremiah 31:31-34 alongside Luke 22:20 and Hebrews 8:8-13. What is "new" about the new covenant, and how do the New Testament writers see it fulfilled?
In Jeremiah 20:7-18 the prophet both praises God and curses the day he was born. What does it mean to you that such honest prayers are part of Scripture?
Jeremiah buys a field in a city under siege (Jeremiah 32:6-15). Where might God be asking you or your church to act in hope when circumstances look bleak?

title: Dead Sea Scrolls
summary: Ancient Jewish manuscripts found from 1947 in eleven caves near Qumran on the north-western shore of the Dead Sea, dating from about the third century BC to AD 68; they include the oldest known copies of the books of the Hebrew Bible, alongside other religious writings of the Second Temple period.
studyQuestions: Every book of the Hebrew Bible except one is represented among the scrolls. Which book is missing, and why might the absence of a book from a small, damaged collection prove very little?
Compare Deuteronomy 32:8 in two English translations. How do they end the verse, and what does the difference tell you about the manuscripts behind them?
Both the Qumran community and Mark 1:2-3 used Isaiah 40:3 about the wilderness. How did each understand the "way" being prepared?
How does it affect your confidence in Scripture to learn that a scroll copied before Jesus's birth reads almost exactly like the Isaiah in your Bible, while also showing small differences?

title: Deuteronomy
summary: The fifth book of the Bible and the last book of the Torah (Pentateuch), presented as Moses' farewell speeches to Israel on the plains of Moab, in which he recalls the covenant made at Horeb (Sinai), restates its laws, calls Israel to love the one God with all their heart, and sets before them the choice of life or death before he dies and Joshua leads them into the land.
studyQuestions: Where and when does Moses speak, according to Deuteronomy 1:1-5? Why might it matter that the people are standing on the edge of the land rather than at Sinai?

In Deuteronomy 5:2-3 Moses says the covenant at Horeb was made "with us, even us, who are all of us here alive today". Most of his listeners were born after Sinai. What is he asking them to understand about God's covenant, and how might that apply to a reader today?
Read the Shema (Deuteronomy 6:4-9). List the places and times of day where God's words are to be kept. What would that look like in your household or small group?
Deuteronomy 30:11-14 says the commandment is "not too hard" and "very near". How does that sit with the warnings in the rest of the chapter?
When Jesus is tempted in the wilderness (Matthew 4:1-11), every answer he gives comes from Deuteronomy. Why do you think he reached for this book in particular?
Moses sees the land but does not enter it (Deuteronomy 34:4-5). What does his story teach about faithfulness when we do not see the end of what God is doing?

title: Forgiveness in the Bible
summary: What Scripture says to Christians who need to forgive, or to be forgiven: God's forgiveness of sin, freely given and proclaimed from Exodus 34 to the cross, and Jesus's call for his followers to forgive others from the heart as they have been forgiven, without pretending that harm did not happen.
studyQuestions: How does God describe himself to Moses in Exodus 34:6-7, and what does that tell us about where forgiveness begins?
In Matthew 18:21-35, how large is the first servant's debt compared with what his fellow servant owes him, and what point is Jesus making by the contrast?
Luke 17:3-4 speaks of rebuking a brother who sins and forgiving him when he repents. How does that fit with Jesus praying for those crucifying him in Luke 23:34?
What did Joseph's forgiveness of his brothers in Genesis 50:15-21 include, and what did it not pretend?
Is there someone I find hard to forgive? What would it look like to begin by praying for them, even before my feelings change?

title: Genesis
summary: The first book of the Bible and of the Pentateuch (Torah), which tells of God's creation of the world, humanity's fall into sin and its spread, the Flood and Babel, and then God's call of Abraham and the story of his family through Isaac, Jacob and Joseph, ending with Israel's ancestors in Egypt.
studyQuestions: Read Genesis 1:26-28 and 1:31. What does God say about human beings, and how does he judge everything he has made?
Genesis 2:4 and 37:2 both begin with "This is the history of the generations of…". How does noticing this repeated heading help you see the shape of the whole book?
What three things does God promise Abram in Genesis 12:1-3, and who, finally, is to share in the blessing?
In Genesis 50:20 Joseph looks back on his brothers' cruelty. What does he say about their intentions and about God's? Where have you seen God bring good out of something meant for harm?
Paul quotes Genesis 15:6 in Romans 4:3 and Genesis 12:3 in Galatians 3:8. Why do you think the apostle reaches back to Genesis to explain the gospel?
Genesis opens with a world declared "very good" and closes with a family in a foreign land waiting for God's promise. What does that tell you about where the story is heading?

title: Genre in the Bible
summary: The interpretive habit of noticing what kind of writing a passage is (story, law, song, proverb, prophecy, gospel, letter or apocalypse) and reading it by the rules of that kind, so that we hear what its author meant in the way he meant it.
studyQuestions: Read Exodus 14:21-31 and then Exodus 15:1-10. What does the song add to the narrative account of the same event?
Psalm 98:8 calls on rivers to clap their hands. What is the psalmist inviting us to see and do?
How does Luke describe his purpose in Luke 1:1-4, and what does that tell you about the kind of book he is writing?
Revelation 1:1-4 calls the book a revelation, a prophecy and (by its greeting) a letter. How might each of these shape the way you read it?
Which part of the Bible do you find hardest to read, and could knowing more about its kind of writing help?
steps: Before interpreting a passage, ask what kind of writing it is (narrative, law, poetry, proverb, prophecy, gospel, letter or apocalypse) and look for clues the book gives about itself.
Note the features of that kind of writing, such as parallel lines and imagery in poetry, short general sayings in proverbs, or greetings and arguments in letters.
Ask what that kind of writing is designed to do (tell what happened, command, praise, give practical wisdom, warn, comfort or encourage endurance) and let that purpose guide your conclusions.
Compare passages where the Bible tells the same thing in two forms, such as the Red Sea in Exodus 14 and 15, and notice what each form adds.
Check your genre judgment with a study Bible or Bible dictionary, and hold it humbly where careful readers disagree.
Apply the passage in a way that fits its genre, taking a promise as a promise, a proverb as wise counsel and a song as praise to join.

example.situation: A small-group member reads Proverbs 26:4 and 26:5 side by side and concludes that the Bible contradicts itself.
example.before: Verse 4 says don't answer a fool and verse 5 says answer him, so one of these must be wrong, and Proverbs can't be trusted.
example.after: These are proverbs, not laws. Placed side by side, they teach that sometimes silence is wise and sometimes a reply is needed, and wisdom lies in discerning which situation I am in.
example.why: Proverbs are short sayings that capture general truths for particular situations; reading them as rigid rules or guarantees misses how the genre works.

title: The Giving of the Law at Sinai
summary: The encounter at Mount Sinai (Horeb) in Exodus 19-24, where God came down on the mountain in fire and cloud, spoke the Ten Commandments to the Israelites he had just rescued from Egypt, gave his laws through Moses, and bound Israel to himself in a covenant sealed with blood.
studyQuestions: In Exodus 19:4-6, what does God remind Israel he has already done, and what does he say they will become if they keep his covenant?
Why do the people ask Moses to speak to them instead of God (Exodus 20:18-21; Deuteronomy 5:23-27)? What does Moses say the fear is meant to do?
What happens with the blood in Exodus 24:6-8, and how do Jesus's words over the cup in Mark 14:24 echo Moses' words?
Deuteronomy 5:3 tells a later generation that the covenant was made "with us". In what sense does a story that happened long ago become your story too?
Hebrews 12:18-24 contrasts Sinai with Mount Zion. How should both the holiness of Sinai and the welcome of Zion shape the way you come to God in worship?

title: Gospel of Luke
summary: The third Gospel and the first volume of Luke's two-part work with Acts: an orderly account, written for Theophilus, of Jesus' birth, Spirit-anointed ministry, long journey to Jerusalem, death, resurrection and ascension, presenting him as the Saviour who seeks and saves the lost and brings good news to the poor and to all peoples.
studyQuestions: Read Luke 1:1-4. What does Luke say about how he gathered his material, and why does he say he is writing to Theophilus?
In the synagogue at Nazareth (Luke 4:16-21) Jesus reads from Isaiah 61. Who is the good news for, and what does he say has happened "today"?

Luke 15 opens with a complaint that Jesus "receiveth sinners, and eateth with them" (15:2). How do the three stories that follow answer it, and why does the last one end with the elder brother still outside?
In Luke 10:29 the lawyer asks "who is my neighbor?", but in 10:36 Jesus asks which man "proved neighbor". How does that change of question change the way you read the parable?
Luke 24 ends with the risen Jesus opening the Scriptures to his disciples (24:27, 44-45). How might reading the Old Testament "concerning himself" shape the way you read it this week?

title: Gospel of Mark
summary: The second and shortest of the four Gospels, and by wide agreement the earliest: a fast-moving account of "the gospel of Jesus Christ, the Son of God" that follows his ministry of authority in Galilee, his road to Jerusalem and his death and empty tomb, and calls readers to take up the cross and follow him; tradition links it to John Mark and the preaching of Peter.
studyQuestions: Mark calls Jesus "the Son of God" in his first verse (1:1). Who else says so, or something like it, at 1:11, 9:7 and 15:39, and why might it matter that the last voice is a Roman centurion at the cross?
In Mark 8:29-31 Peter confesses "Thou art the Christ," and Jesus at once begins to teach that the Son of Man must suffer. Why do you think the two belong together, and what did Peter get wrong?
Read Mark 10:45. What does it say the Son of Man came to do, and how does it explain the request of James and John just before it (10:35-44)?

The oldest manuscripts end at 16:8 with the women saying "nothing to any one; for they were afraid" (ASV). What is the young man's message in 16:7, and what might an ending like this ask of the reader?

Mark shows the disciples misunderstanding, failing and running away, yet Jesus sends word to "his disciples and Peter" (16:7). What encouragement does that give to people who follow Jesus imperfectly?

title: Gospel of Matthew
summary: The first book of the New Testament: an account of the life, teaching, death and resurrection of Jesus that presents him as Israel's Messiah, Son of David and Son of God, organised around five great teaching discourses and closing with the commission to make disciples of all nations.
studyQuestions: Matthew 1:1 calls Jesus "the son of David, the son of Abraham." Why might Matthew open with those two names in particular?
Find the sentence that closes each of the five teaching blocks (Matthew 7:28, 11:1, 13:53, 19:1 and 26:1). What does each discourse teach disciples about life in the kingdom?
In Matthew 5:17-20, what does Jesus say he came to do with the Law and the Prophets, and what kind of righteousness does he ask of his followers?
The Gospel begins with "God with us" (1:23) and ends with "I am with you always" (28:20). How does that promise frame everything in between, and where do you need to hear it this week?

title: The Four Gospels
summary: The four books that open the New Testament (Matthew, Mark, Luke and John), each telling the good news of Jesus Christ's life, teaching, death and resurrection from its own angle, and received together by the church since the second century as one fourfold witness to him.
studyQuestions: Mark 1:1 calls what follows "the beginning of the gospel of Jesus Christ". What does the word "gospel" mean, and where in Isaiah 40 and 52 does the idea of a messenger with good news come from?
According to Luke 1:1-4, what did Luke know about earlier accounts and eyewitnesses, and why did he write his own?
John 20:30-31 says many signs were left out. What does John say his book is for, and how might that purpose shape the way you read any of the Gospels?
Paul summarises "the gospel" in 1 Corinthians 15:1-5. Which of those events do all four Gospels tell at length, and why do you think they give them so much space?
Choose one story told in more than one Gospel. Read the versions side by side. What does each writer emphasise, and what would be lost if we merged them into one account?

title: Grace
summary: God's free, undeserved favour and the gift of his saving and transforming life, traced in Scripture from God's favour to Noah and his self-description as "merciful and gracious" in Exodus 34 to the grace that comes through Jesus Christ and saves "through faith"; Christian traditions agree that salvation begins in grace but describe how grace works in different ways.
studyQuestions: Exodus 34:6 is God's own description of himself to Moses. Which words in it describe grace, and why is it striking that this comes right after the golden calf?
According to Ephesians 2:8-10, what saves us, what does not, and what are we then created for?
In Romans 6:1-2, what wrong conclusion does Paul expect someone to draw from "grace abounded", and how does he answer it?
Paul hears "My grace is sufficient for you" in a time of weakness (2 Corinthians 12:9). Where in your own life, or your church's, do you most need grace as strength rather than only as pardon?
Each Christian tradition says that salvation begins with God's grace. How might that shared conviction change the way you talk with Christians of another tradition?

title: Inductive Bible Study
summary: A way of studying a passage or book of the Bible that begins with careful observation of what the text actually says, moves to interpreting what it means in its context, correlates it with the rest of Scripture, and ends in applying it to life.
studyQuestions: According to Acts 17:10-12, what did the Jews of Beroea do with Paul's message, and how often?
Ezra 7:10 describes Ezra's commitment to God's law in three verbs. What are they, and why might the order matter?
James 1:22-25 compares a hearer who does not act to someone looking in a mirror. What point is James making about study and application?
Read Mark 4:35-41 slowly and list everything you observe before deciding what it means. What did you notice that you had missed before?
Which of the phases (observation, interpretation, correlation, application) do you tend to skip, and how could your group help you slow down?
steps: Pray for understanding, then choose a unit to study (a paragraph, a chapter or a whole short book) and read it through several times without notes or commentary.
Observe before you explain - write down who is involved, what happens or is argued, where and when, and note repeated words, contrasts, questions, turning points and the kind of writing it is.
Turn your observations into questions (what does this mean, why is it here, why is it said this way?) and answer them first from the passage and its surrounding book.
Only after your own study, check your conclusions against a good study Bible, Bible dictionary or commentary, and revise where the evidence points elsewhere.
Correlate the passage with the rest of Scripture, asking how other texts on the same subject, and the whole story centred on Christ, shed light on it.
Ask what the passage meant for its first readers and what it calls you to believe, pray or do now, and write down one concrete response.
Share what you found with others, ideally in a small group, so that your reading can be tested and enriched.

example.situation: A small group opens Mark 4:35-41, the stilling of the storm, during a hard season for one of its members.
example.before: This story promises that Jesus will make the storms in my life go away if I have enough faith.
example.after: The disciples end by asking who Jesus is, since even wind and sea obey him; the passage first shows his identity and calls me to trust him in the storm, whether or not it stops.
example.why: Observing the closing question (Mark 4:41) and its echo of God calming the sea in Psalm 107:29 moves the group from a quick application to the passage's own focus on who Jesus is.

title: Israelites
summary: The people descended, in the biblical account, from Jacob (renamed Israel) through his twelve sons; brought out of Egypt and bound to God by covenant at Sinai, they are the chosen people whose story fills the Old Testament and whose heritage Paul treasures in Romans 9–11.
studyQuestions: Why does Jacob receive the new name "Israel" in Genesis 32:28, and what does God promise him when he confirms the name in Genesis 35:9-12?
According to Deuteronomy 7:6-9, why did God choose Israel, and what was not the reason?
What does God ask of Israel in Exodus 19:5-6, and what does he say Israel will become?
In Romans 9:4-5 Paul lists the gifts that belong to the Israelites. Which of these gifts have reached you, and how might that shape the way you speak about the Jewish people?
Israel was not chosen for being large or impressive (Deuteronomy 7:7). How does it change your sense of belonging to God to know that his choice rests on love rather than merit?

title: Jeremiah's Temple Sermon
aliases: Jeremiah's sermon at the temple gate
the temple of the LORD sermon
summary: Jeremiah's message at the gate of the Jerusalem Temple (Jeremiah 7:1-15, with the story of its aftermath in Jeremiah 26), warning worshippers that chanting "the temple of the LORD" would not protect people who oppressed the vulnerable and broke the covenant, and that God could make the Temple like ruined Shiloh unless they changed their ways.
studyQuestions: Where does God tell Jeremiah to stand in Jeremiah 7:2, and who would be passing by as he spoke?
What were the people repeating in Jeremiah 7:4 and 7:10, and why did those words feel like a guarantee of safety?
Which wrongs does Jeremiah list in 7:5-9? How do they line up with the Ten Commandments and with care for the foreigner, the fatherless and the widow?
Why does God send the listeners to look at Shiloh (7:12-14)? What had happened there?
In Jeremiah 26 the elders remember Micah's words about Zion (26:18-19). How does that memory save Jeremiah's life, and what does it suggest about how God's warnings work?
Jesus quotes Jeremiah 7:11 in the Temple (Mark 11:17). What does the original sermon add to your understanding of that scene?
What "safe words" or religious habits might a church or a believer lean on today instead of a changed life, and how could this passage gently correct that?

title: Jerusalem
summary: The hill city in the Judean highlands that David captured from the Jebusites and made his capital, where Solomon built the Temple; the centre of Israel's worship, the place of Jesus' death and resurrection and the starting point of the church's mission, and in the prophets and Revelation an image of God's people and his future dwelling with them.
studyQuestions: According to 2 Samuel 5:6-9, who lived in Jerusalem before David, and what did David call the stronghold once he took it?
Read Psalm 122. Why were pilgrims glad to go up to Jerusalem, and what does the psalmist ask readers to pray for?
In Isaiah 2:2-4, who comes to Jerusalem in the "latter days", and what do they go away with?
Luke 9:51 says Jesus "intently set his face" to go to Jerusalem, and Luke 19:41-44 shows him weeping over it. What do these two moments tell you about how Jesus regarded the city?
Revelation 21 describes a New Jerusalem with no temple in it. What does that suggest about where God means to live, and how might that hope shape the way you worship now?

title: Kingdom of God
summary: God's active reign as King, celebrated in the Old Testament, announced by Jesus as "at hand" in his own words and deeds, and awaited in its fullness when God's will is done on earth as in heaven; the central theme of Jesus's preaching in the first three Gospels.
studyQuestions: According to Mark 1:14-15, what does Jesus announce when he begins preaching in Galilee, and what two responses does he ask for?
In Luke 11:20, what does Jesus point to as a sign that God's Kingdom "has come to you"?
What do the parables of the seed growing by itself and the mustard seed (Mark 4:26-32) suggest about how God's Kingdom grows, and who makes it grow?
Psalm 145:13 calls God's Kingdom everlasting, yet Jesus teaches us to pray "Let your Kingdom come" (Matthew 6:10). How can both be true?
When you pray the Lord's Prayer, where in your own life, family or church do you most long to see God's will done "as in heaven, so on earth"?

title: Laying the Foundation of the Second Temple
aliases: rebuilding of the altar after the exile
joy and weeping at the Temple foundation
summary: Ezra 3:1-13, where the exiles who returned from Babylon rebuild the altar, keep the Feast of Tabernacles, and lay the foundation of a new Temple in Jerusalem, while the old who remembered Solomon's Temple weep and the young shout for joy so that the two sounds cannot be told apart.
studyQuestions: According to Ezra 3:2-6, what did the returned exiles build first, and what did they begin doing even though the Temple's foundation "was not yet laid"?
Ezra 3:3 says the people built the altar while "fear was on them". What does it suggest that they worshipped anyway?
What did the priests and Levites sing when the foundation was laid (Ezra 3:11), and where else in Scripture does that refrain appear?
Why did the older priests and Levites weep in Ezra 3:12? How does Haggai 2:3-9 speak to the same feeling?

Have you known a moment, in your own life or your church's, when joy and grief were mixed together so that you "could not discern" one from the other? What does this passage give you to bring to such a moment?

title: Lectio Divina
summary: An ancient Christian way of reading a short passage of Scripture slowly and prayerfully, moving through reading (lectio), meditation (meditatio), prayer (oratio) and contemplation (contemplatio), and often on to action (actio), so that reading the Bible becomes a conversation with God.
studyQuestions: According to Psalm 1:1-3, where does the blessed person find delight, and what picture describes the result of meditating day and night?
Joshua 1:8 says the book of the law should not depart from Joshua's mouth. What does that suggest about how meditation was practised, and what is it meant to lead to?
What did Mary do with the shepherds' words in Luke 2:19, and how is that like the step of meditatio?
In Luke 10:38-42, what is Mary doing, what is Martha doing, and why does Jesus defend Mary?
Which movement (reading, meditation, prayer, contemplation or action) comes hardest for you, and how could a small group help you grow in it?
steps: Choose a short passage of a few verses, such as a Gospel scene or a psalm, settle into quiet, and ask God to speak to you through his word.
Lectio - read the passage slowly several times, aloud if you can, and first ask what the text says in itself and where it sits in its chapter.
Meditatio - stay with a word or phrase that stands out, turn it over, and ask what that meaning says to your life today.
Oratio - answer God in your own words, with thanks, confession, questions or requests drawn from the passage.
Contemplatio - rest quietly before God for a few minutes without trying to produce more thoughts.
Actio - choose one concrete way to live out what you received, and test any strong impression against the wider Bible and with your church or small group.

example.situation: A member of a small group prays through Luke 10:38-42, the visit of Jesus to Martha and Mary, during a busy season of church volunteering.
example.before: Jesus' words to Martha about the one thing needed jumped out at me, so God is telling me to quit the hospitality team.
example.after: In the scene, Jesus defends Mary for sitting and listening to him while Martha is pulled apart by her serving; he invites me to put listening to him first and to notice where worry crowds it out, and my serving can grow from that.
example.why: Lectio begins by asking what the text says in itself before asking what it says to me, so a striking phrase is heard within its scene instead of as a free-floating private message.

title: The Lord's Prayer
summary: The prayer Jesus taught his disciples, given in a longer form in the Sermon on the Mount (Matthew 6:9-13) and a shorter one in Luke 11:2-4: an address to God as Father followed by petitions for his name, kingdom and will, and for daily bread, forgiveness and deliverance — prayed by Christians of every tradition ever since.
studyQuestions: Compare Matthew 6:9-13 with Luke 11:2-4. Which petitions do both share, and what setting does each Gospel give the prayer (Matthew 6:5-8; Luke 11:1)?
The first petitions are about God's name, kingdom and will; the later ones about our bread, our sins and our testing. What does that order teach about how to pray?
Every pronoun in the prayer is plural ("our", "us"). How does praying it change if I picture my church, or the believers I find hardest to love, praying it with me?
In Matthew 6:14-15 Jesus adds a comment on just one petition. Which one, and why might he single it out?
Jesus prays "your desire be done" in Gethsemane (Matthew 26:42). How does that scene deepen what it means to pray "your will be done"?

title: Loving Your Neighbor
summary: What Scripture says to Christians asking how to treat the people around them: the command of Leviticus 19:18 to love one's neighbor as oneself, which Jesus set beside love for God as the heart of the law, widened through the parable of the Good Samaritan and the call to love enemies, and which the apostles called the fulfilment of the law.
studyQuestions: Read Leviticus 19:9-18. Which concrete actions does the chapter list before it reaches "love your neighbor as yourself," and what do they show about what love means there?
In Luke 10:29 the lawyer asks "Who is my neighbor?" How does Jesus's question in Luke 10:36 turn that question around?
According to Romans 13:8-10 and Galatians 5:14, how is love of neighbor related to the rest of God's commandments?
What does 1 John 4:20-21 say about someone who claims to love God but hates a brother or sister?
Who is a "neighbor" I find easy to pass by, at church, at work or on my street, and what is one act of mercy I could offer this week?

title: Masoretic Text
summary: The traditional Hebrew text of the Old Testament as fixed by Jewish scholars called Masoretes between about the sixth and tenth centuries AD, who added vowel signs, reading accents and marginal notes to the inherited consonantal text; it is the authoritative Bible of Judaism and the basis of most modern Old Testament translations.
studyQuestions: Read Psalm 100:3 in the King James Version and in the World English Bible. How do they differ, and how does the Masoretic note about what is "written" and what is "read" explain it?
In Nehemiah 8:8 the Levites read the law "distinctly" and "gave the sense". How did the Masoretes' vowel signs and accents serve the same goal?
According to Luke 4:16-17, what was Jesus handed in the synagogue at Nazareth, and what does that tell you about how Scripture was read in his day?
Why might the Masoretes have counted the verses, words and even letters of Scripture? What does that care suggest about how they regarded the text?
How does it shape your trust in the Old Testament to know that much of it reached your Bible through generations of Jewish scribes?

title: Mosaic Covenant
summary: The covenant God made with Israel through Moses after the Exodus, sealed at Sinai (Exodus 19-24), renewed on the plains of Moab (Deuteronomy 29) and in later generations, binding the rescued people to the Lord with his law, the Sabbath as its sign, and blessings and curses; the prophets foresaw a new covenant, and Christian traditions differ on how its law applies to believers today.
studyQuestions: According to Deuteronomy 7:7-8, why did the Lord choose Israel and bring them out of Egypt? What does that order (love first, commandments after) tell you about the covenant?
What is the sign of this covenant in Exodus 31:13-17, and what two things does keeping it remind Israel of?
Leviticus 26 and Deuteronomy 28-30 set out blessings and curses. What does God promise in Leviticus 26:44-45 and Deuteronomy 30:6 even after the covenant has been broken?
In Deuteronomy 29:14-15 Moses says the covenant is made also with those "not here with us this day". How do Joshua 24 and 2 Kings 23 show later generations taking it up as their own?

Jeremiah 31:32-33 says the new covenant will be "not according to" the one made at the Exodus. What exactly is new, and what stays the same? How does that shape the way you read the laws of Exodus and Leviticus?

title: Moses
summary: The Levite raised in Pharaoh's household whom God called at the burning bush to lead Israel out of Egypt; he mediated the covenant and the law at Sinai, interceded for the people through forty years in the wilderness and died within sight of the promised land, remembered as the prophet with whom the LORD spoke face to face.
studyQuestions: According to Exodus 3:7-12, what has God seen and heard, what will he do, and how does he answer Moses' question "Who am I"?
What excuse does Moses give in Exodus 4:10, and how does God respond in verses 11-17?
In Exodus 32:11-14 and 32:30-32, what reasons does Moses give God for sparing the people? What does his prayer show about the kind of leader he was?
Why was Moses not allowed to lead Israel into the land (Numbers 20:7-12)? What exactly had God told him to do, and what did he do instead?
Hebrews 3:5-6 calls Moses a faithful servant in God's house and Christ a faithful Son over it. How does that comparison honour Moses rather than dismiss him?
Moses argued with God, failed, interceded and kept going for forty years. Where in your own calling do you most identify with his reluctance — or with his perseverance?

title: New Testament
summary: The second part of the Christian Bible: 27 books written in Greek in the first Christian generations (four Gospels, Acts, 21 letters and Revelation) that tell of Jesus Christ and the earliest church, and that Catholic, Orthodox and Protestant Christians all receive as Scripture.
studyQuestions: What does Jesus call the cup in Luke 22:20, and how does that explain the name "New Testament"?
Which Old Testament promise does Hebrews 8 quote from verse 8 onward, and what does the writer conclude from it in verse 13?
According to Luke 1:1-4, how did Luke go about writing his Gospel, and why?
What do Colossians 4:16 and 2 Peter 3:15-16 show about how the first churches shared and regarded the apostles' letters?
John 20:31 gives a purpose for John's Gospel. Could the same purpose describe the whole New Testament? Which of its books have you read least, and how might you begin?

title: Old Testament
summary: The first and larger part of the Christian Bible: the Scriptures of Israel, written mostly in Hebrew with some Aramaic, that Jesus and the apostles read as God's word, running from Genesis to Malachi in 39 books for Protestants and with additional deuterocanonical books for Catholics and the Orthodox.
studyQuestions: According to Luke 24:27 and 24:44, which parts of Israel's Scriptures did the risen Jesus say were about him?
What does God promise in Jeremiah 31:31-33, and how does that promise explain why Christians speak of an "old" and a "new" testament?
In 2 Timothy 3:15, Timothy had known the sacred writings from infancy. Which writings could those have been, and what does Paul say they can do?
Romans 15:4 says earlier Scripture was written "for our learning." Which Old Testament book has taught you the most, and which have you barely opened?
How could you speak about the "Old" Testament in a way that honours both its lasting value for Christians and its place as Jewish Scripture?

title: Parable of the Good Samaritan
summary: Jesus's story in Luke 10:25-37, told to a lawyer who asked "Who is my neighbor?", about a man left half dead on the road down to Jericho who is passed by a priest and a Levite and rescued by a Samaritan; Jesus ends by asking who proved a neighbor and telling the lawyer to "go and do likewise."
studyQuestions: What two commandments does the lawyer quote in Luke 10:27, and where in the law of Moses do they come from (Deuteronomy 6:5; Leviticus 19:18)?
The lawyer asks "Who is my neighbor?" (Luke 10:29), but Jesus asks which of the three "seemed to be a neighbor" (Luke 10:36). What changes between the two questions?
List everything the Samaritan does in Luke 10:33-35. What does each action cost him in time, money or risk?
Read Luke 9:51-56 just before the parable. How might that scene have shaped the way the disciples heard a story with a Samaritan as its hero?
Why is it a misreading to treat the priest and the Levite as a picture of Judaism as a whole?
Who is lying "by the side of the road" in my own week, and what keeps me from crossing over to them?

title: Parables of Jesus
summary: The short, true-to-life stories and comparisons (Greek parabolē, Hebrew mashal) through which Jesus taught in the Synoptic Gospels, mostly about the Kingdom of God, drawing hearers into a story and then turning it on them so they must decide how to respond.
studyQuestions: According to Mark 4:33-34, how did Jesus use parables with the crowds, and what did he do differently with his disciples?
In Matthew 13:10-17, why does Jesus say he speaks in parables, and which prophet's words does he apply to his hearers?
Read 2 Samuel 12:1-7. How does Nathan's story get past David's defences, and what happens when David judges the rich man?
Compare the vineyard in Isaiah 5:1-7 with the vineyard in Mark 12:1-12. What would Jesus's hearers have recognised, and why did they realise the parable was "against them" (Mark 12:12)?
Luke 15:1-3 tells us who was listening when Jesus told the parables of the lost. How does that audience change the way you read the elder brother?
Which parable has most unsettled you, and what was it asking you to decide?

title: Paul
summary: Saul of Tarsus, a Pharisee who persecuted the first Christians, met the risen Jesus on the road to Damascus and became the apostle to the Gentiles; he planted churches across the eastern Mediterranean, and the letters bearing his name make up nearly half the books of the New Testament.
studyQuestions: In Acts 9:1-6, what is Saul doing when Jesus meets him, and what question does Jesus ask him?
Compare Acts 9:20-30 with Galatians 1:15-24. What does each account emphasise about what Paul did after his conversion?
In Philippians 3:4-8, which credentials does Paul list, and how does he now value them?
Paul calls himself "the least of the apostles" yet says God's grace was not in vain (1 Corinthians 15:9-10). How might his story shape the way we see people who have done harm, or our own past?

title: Paul at the Areopagus
summary: Paul's visit to Athens and his speech before the Areopagus in Acts 17:16-34, where he takes an altar "to the unknown god" as his starting point and proclaims the Creator who does not live in temples, who made all nations, and who now calls everyone to repent before the day he will judge the world through the man he raised from the dead.
studyQuestions: What did Paul see in Athens that "stirred" his spirit (Acts 17:16), and where did he go to talk with people (17:17)?
Why did some listeners think Paul was proclaiming "strange gods" (17:18)? What two things had he been preaching?
Paul quotes a Greek poet in Acts 17:28. What point does he draw from the line in the next verse (17:29)?
The speech begins with creation and ends with repentance, judgment and the resurrection (17:30-31). Why do you think Paul builds toward Jesus in that order for this audience?
Luke records three responses in 17:32-34. Which response do you see most often when you talk about faith with friends or colleagues, and what might Paul's example teach you about those conversations?

title: Pharisees
summary: A Jewish movement of the Second Temple period known for careful interpretation and practice of the Torah, the "tradition of the elders" and belief in the resurrection; Jesus's frequent conversation partners and critics in the Gospels, Paul's own party, and forerunners of the later rabbis.
studyQuestions: According to Acts 23:6-8, which beliefs did the Pharisees hold that the Sadducees rejected?
In Matthew 23:2-3, what does Jesus tell the crowds to do with the Pharisees' teaching, and what does he warn them not to copy?
Nicodemus (John 3:1-2) and Gamaliel (Acts 5:34-39) were both Pharisees. How do their stories complicate the picture of the Pharisees as simply Jesus's enemies?
Jesus's sharpest warnings were aimed at devout, Bible-loving people. Where might Matthew 23:23-28 speak to our own church life today?

title: Psalm 22
aliases: My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?
summary: The psalm of David that begins "My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?": a lament that moves from feeling abandoned, mocked and surrounded to a vow of praise in which the nations and generations yet unborn turn to God. Jesus prayed its first words from the cross, and the Gospels tell the crucifixion in its language.
studyQuestions: In Psalm 22:1-2 the psalmist says God does not answer. Whom is he still speaking to, and what does it mean that he calls God "my God"?
What does the psalmist remember in verses 4-5 and 9-10? How do those memories help him keep praying?
Find the point where the psalm turns from plea to praise. How far does the praise reach by verses 27-31?
Compare Psalm 22:7-8 and 22:18 with Matthew 27:35, 39 and 43 and John 19:23-24. What do the Gospel writers want readers to notice?
Jesus prays the first line of this psalm from the cross (Mark 15:34). How does knowing the whole psalm shape the way you hear his cry?
Is there a time when you felt God was far away? What would it look like to pray that honestly, as this psalm does?

title: Reading in Context
aliases: a text without a context is a pretext
summary: The basic interpretive habit of reading any verse within its surrounding passage, its book, the whole of Scripture and its original historical and cultural setting, so that it means what its author meant before we ask what it means for us.
studyQuestions: According to Jeremiah 29:1-10, who first received the letter containing verse 11, where were they, and how long did God say they would wait?
Read Philippians 4:10-14. What "all things" is Paul talking about in verse 13, and how does that change the way the verse is often used?
Revelation 3:20 is often used in evangelism. To whom is it first addressed (Revelation 3:14-22), and what does that add to its meaning?
Which verse do you hold dear but have never read in its surrounding chapter, and what do you notice when you read the whole chapter this week?
steps: Read the whole paragraph, and then the whole chapter, around the verse before deciding what it means.
Ask who is speaking, to whom, and in what situation; note what the book itself tells you about its author and first readers.
Trace the flow of thought by asking what comes just before, what comes just after, and how the verse fits the argument or story.
Identify the kind of writing (letter, poem, prophecy, narrative) and read it the way that kind of writing is meant to be read.
Use a study Bible or Bible dictionary to fill in historical and cultural background, without letting the background drown out the text.
Compare the passage with other Scripture on the same subject, especially clearer passages, and see how it fits the whole story that centres on Christ.
Only then ask what the passage means for you or your church, applying it in a way its first readers would recognise as faithful to it.

example.situation: A friend facing a job interview posts Jeremiah 29:11 as a guarantee that everything will go well.
example.before: God has promised me success and no setbacks, so this interview is bound to work out.
example.after: God told exiles in Babylon to settle in and seek the city's peace, promising a future after seventy years; I can trust his good purposes and be faithful where I am, even if this interview fails.
example.why: Reading the whole letter (Jeremiah 29:1-14) shows a promise of long-range hope to a community in exile, which still comforts believers today but not as a pledge of quick personal success.

title: Sadducees
summary: A small, aristocratic Jewish party of the Second Temple period, closely tied to the high priesthood and the Jerusalem Temple, which held to the written law of Moses, rejected the Pharisees' oral traditions and denied the resurrection of the dead; in the Gospels they question Jesus about the resurrection, and in Acts they lead opposition to the apostles.
studyQuestions: In Mark 12:18-27, what question do the Sadducees put to Jesus, and which passage of the Law of Moses does he answer them from?
According to Acts 23:8, what three things did the Sadducees deny, and how does Paul use that disagreement in Acts 23:6-10?
Why were the priests and the Sadducees "upset" with Peter and John in Acts 4:1-2?
Jesus tells the Sadducees they know neither "the Scriptures nor the power of God" (Mark 12:24). How might sincere Bible readers today make a similar mistake, and what helps guard against it?

title: The Sadducees' Question about the Resurrection
summary: The Synoptic scene in the Jerusalem Temple (Mark 12:18-27; Matthew 22:23-33; Luke 20:27-40) in which Sadducees, who denied the resurrection, pose a riddle about a widow married to seven brothers, and Jesus answers that the risen do not marry and that God's words to Moses at the burning bush show he is "the God of the living."
studyQuestions: Which law of Moses do the Sadducees build their question on (compare Mark 12:19 with Deuteronomy 25:5-6), and what was that law meant to protect?
Jesus says the Sadducees know neither "the Scriptures nor the power of God" (Mark 12:24). Which part of his answer addresses each of those two mistakes?
Read Exodus 3:6 and Mark 12:26-27 side by side. Why does God's naming himself "the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob" matter for whether the dead will be raised?
Luke adds that "all are alive to him" (Luke 20:38). How might that line shape the way a Christian thinks about believers who have died?
Does Jesus say that the risen become angels, or that they are like angels? Why does the difference matter?

title: Scripture Interprets Scripture
summary: The interpretive principle that the Bible is its own best interpreter: a passage is read in the light of the rest of Scripture, with clearer passages shedding light on harder ones, so that no single verse is made to say what the whole Bible does not.
studyQuestions: In Matthew 4:1-11, where do Jesus's replies in verses 4 and 7 come from, and what situation of Israel's were those words first spoken into?
What does the devil leave out when he uses Psalm 91 in Matthew 4:6, and what difference does Deuteronomy 6:16 make?
According to Luke 24:27 and 24:44-45, how did the risen Jesus help his disciples understand the Scriptures as a whole?
What did the people of Beroea do with Paul's preaching in Acts 17:11, and what would it look like for your study group to do the same?
Is there a verse you have built a lot on by itself? Which other passages on the same subject could you read alongside it this week?
steps: Read the passage in its own setting first (paragraph, chapter, book) so you know what it says before you compare it with anything else.
Look up the cross-references in a study Bible, starting with any passage the text quotes or echoes, and read each one in its own context too.
When the New Testament quotes the Old, open the Old Testament passage and ask what it meant there and why the New Testament writer reached for it.
Gather the passages that treat the same subject directly and at length, and let these clearer, fuller passages shed light on brief or puzzling ones.
Check that each link is a real link of meaning, not just a shared English word that may mean different things in different books.
When passages seem to pull in different directions, hold both and ask how they fit together before choosing one and setting the other aside.
Test your conclusion against the main lines of the whole biblical story and, as your church teaches, against its wider reading of the faith.

example.situation: Someone reads Psalm 91:11-12, "they will bear you up in their hands", and concludes that God guarantees protection from the consequences of any deliberate risk they choose to take.
example.before: God promised his angels will catch me, so I can push my luck and he has to rescue me.
example.after: Psalm 91 is a song of trust for the one who makes God their refuge; Jesus, offered this very verse as a dare, answered from Deuteronomy 6:16 that we must not put God to the test.
example.why: In Matthew 4:5-7 the devil quotes the psalm on its own, and Jesus answers "Again, it is written", letting another Scripture show how the promise is meant to be held.

title: Second Temple Judaism
aliases: Judaism of the Second Temple period
the Jews' religion in Jesus's day
summary: The faith and life of the Jewish people from the rebuilding of the Jerusalem Temple (515 BC) to its destruction by Rome (AD 70), centred on the one God, the Torah and the Temple yet varied in its parties and hopes; the world of Ezra, the Maccabees, Jesus, the apostles and Paul.
studyQuestions: According to Nehemiah 8:1-8, what did Ezra and the Levites do with the Law of Moses, and how did the people respond?
In Luke 4:16-21, what does Jesus do "as was his custom" on the Sabbath, and what does that tell us about his own Jewish practice?
Acts 23:6-8 shows Pharisees and Sadducees disagreeing about the resurrection. What does that suggest about how varied Jewish belief was in Paul's day?
Which familiar Gospel scenes (a synagogue reading, a Temple feast, a debate with Pharisees) do you now picture differently, and why might knowing Jesus's Jewish world deepen your reading of him?

title: Septuagint
summary: The ancient Greek translation of Israel's Scriptures, begun with the Pentateuch in Egypt in the third century BC; it was the Bible of Greek-speaking Jews and of the first Christians, is quoted throughout the New Testament, and remains the Old Testament of the Orthodox Church.
studyQuestions: Compare Psalm 40:6 in an English Bible with Hebrews 10:5. What does each say God prepared, and why might they differ?
In Acts 15:17, how does James's quotation of Amos 9:12 support welcoming Gentiles, and how does the Hebrew wording of Amos read?
Why do you think the apostles were content to quote Scripture in a translation their hearers could understand?
How might knowing about the Septuagint help you talk graciously with a Christian whose Old Testament has more books than yours?

title: Sermon on the Mount
summary: Jesus's longest continuous teaching in the Gospels (Matthew 5–7), given on a mountain in Galilee: the Beatitudes, salt and light, the fulfilment of the Law, almsgiving, prayer and fasting, the Lord's Prayer, the Golden Rule and the closing call to hear and do his words.
studyQuestions: Who is listening when Jesus begins to teach in Matthew 5:1-2, and who is listening when he finishes in Matthew 7:28-29? Why might both groups matter?
In Matthew 5:17-20, what does Jesus say he came to do with the Law and the Prophets?
Read the three examples of "secret" devotion in Matthew 6:1-18 (giving, prayer, fasting). What do they have in common, and which one most challenges your own habits?
The sermon ends with two builders (Matthew 7:24-27). What is the difference between them, and what would "doing" one of these teachings look like for you or your group this week?

title: The Shema
summary: Deuteronomy 6:4-9, named for its first Hebrew word ("Hear"): Israel's confession that the LORD is our God and the LORD is one, joined to the command to love him with all the heart, soul and strength and to keep his words in the heart, the home and daily life. It became the central confession of Jewish prayer, and Jesus quoted it as the first commandment.
studyQuestions: Read Deuteronomy 6:4-5. What does Israel confess about God, and what does God ask for in return? Why do you think the command to love follows straight after the confession?
List every place and time of day named in Deuteronomy 6:7-9. Which of them are part of your ordinary week, and how could God's words be "on your heart" there?
In Deuteronomy 6:20-23 a child asks what the commandments mean. How do the parents answer, and what does that suggest about why Israel obeys?
When the scribe asks Jesus which commandment is first (Mark 12:28-32), how does Jesus answer, and what does the scribe add?
Paul writes of "one God, the Father" and "one Lord, Jesus Christ" (1 Corinthians 8:6). How does this echo the Shema, and what does it say about who Jesus is?
James 2:19 says even the demons believe that God is one. What is the difference between agreeing with the Shema and living it?

title: The Song of the Sea
summary: The victory hymn of Exodus 15:1-21, sung by Moses and the Israelites and answered by Miriam and the women after the crossing of the sea, praising the LORD as the warrior who saved his people, the incomparable God who redeems and guides them home, and the King who "will reign forever and ever".
studyQuestions: Exodus 14:31 says the people "feared Yahweh" and believed. How does the song that follows in Exodus 15:1 turn that fear and faith into worship?
List the names and pictures the song uses for God in Exodus 15:2-3 and 15:11. Which one surprises you, and why?
Verses 1-12 look back at the sea; verses 13-17 look ahead. Where is God leading his people, according to verses 13 and 17?
What does Exodus 15:18 add to the whole song? How does it prepare you to hear Jesus announce the kingdom of God?
Who is Miriam (Exodus 15:20), and what does it mean that the women answer the song with drums and dancing?
In Revelation 15:3 the redeemed sing "the song of Moses ... and the song of the Lamb". What rescue in your own life or your church's story would you put into words of praise?

title: Suffering and Lament
aliases: where is God when it hurts
summary: What Scripture says to Christians who are suffering: the Bible does not explain every sorrow, but it gives God's people words to bring their pain, protest and questions honestly to him in lament, as the psalmists, Job, Lamentations and Jesus on the cross did, and it holds that cry together with trust in God's faithful love and the hope of a world made new.
studyQuestions: Psalm 13 asks "How long?" four times in two verses. What changes in verses 5-6, and has the psalmist's situation changed by then?
Psalm 88 ends in darkness, without a turn to praise. Why might God have included a prayer like this in Scripture?
In Job 42:7-8, God says the friends did not speak rightly about him "as my servant Job has." What had the friends said, and what had Job done?
Jesus prays the opening words of Psalm 22 from the cross (Matthew 27:46). How does knowing the whole psalm shape the way you hear his cry?
What do I find hardest to say honestly to God? What would it look like to pray a lament psalm in my own words this week?

title: The Exodus
summary: God's deliverance of the Israelites from slavery in Egypt under Moses — through the plagues, the first Passover and the crossing of the sea — which became Israel's defining story of salvation and which the New Testament uses to explain the death and resurrection of Jesus.
studyQuestions: In Exodus 3:7-8, what four things does God say he has seen, heard, known and come down to do for his people?
According to Exodus 12:26-27, what are parents to tell their children when they ask about the Passover, and why might Israel have built a question into the ritual?
How does Exodus 20:2 connect the commandments to the rescue from Egypt? What difference does it make that God saves first and then gives the law?

Paul calls Christ "our Passover" (1 Corinthians 5:7) and says the wilderness events "happened to them by way of example" (1 Corinthians 10:11). Where do you see your own story in Israel's — both the rescue and the grumbling afterwards?

title: The Story of the Bible
summary: The single, unfolding story that Christians read across the Bible's many books: God creates a good world, humanity turns away, God calls Abraham and Israel, comes in Jesus the Messiah, sends the church to all nations, and promises a renewed creation.
studyQuestions: In Genesis 12:1-3, what does God promise Abram, and who will finally be blessed through him?
According to Luke 24:27 and Luke 24:44, which parts of the Scriptures did the risen Jesus say were about him?
Compare Genesis 3:23-24 with Revelation 22:1-3. What was lost at the beginning of the story, and what is restored at the end?
Why might it matter whether the Old Testament closes with Cyrus's call to "go up" (2 Chronicles 36:23) or with the promise of Elijah (Malachi 4:5)?
If the church lives in the "act" between Pentecost and the new creation, what would faithful "improvising" look like in your own congregation this year?

title: The Temple
summary: The sanctuary of Israel's God on the Temple Mount in Jerusalem: first built by Solomon and burned by the Babylonians, rebuilt after the exile and lavishly expanded by Herod, then destroyed by Rome in AD 70; in Scripture the place where God set his name among his people, a theme the New Testament carries over to Jesus himself and to the church.
studyQuestions: According to 2 Samuel 7, David wanted to build God a house. What "house" does God promise to build for David instead, and who will build the Temple?
In 1 Kings 8:27-30, Solomon says heaven itself cannot contain God. If that is so, what was the Temple for, according to his prayer?
In John 2:18-22, what did Jesus mean by "this temple", and when did his disciples finally understand it?

Paul tells the Corinthian church, "ye are the temple of God" (1 Corinthians 3:16, KJV). How might seeing your congregation, and not only a building, as God's dwelling change the way you treat one another?
